Self-hosting

Docker stack, security, deployment

sched is self-hosted by design — a single daemon + SQLite, or the full Docker stack with the web UI (shell).

The daemon image

The official image is built from the published @schedjs/daemon npm package — the artifact that passed the test/parity gates — not from monorepo sources:

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
FROM node:24-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
RUN echo '{"name":"schedd","private":true,"packageManager":"yarn@4.18.0"}' > package.json \
 && corepack enable \
 && printf 'nodeLinker: node-modules\nnpmMinimalAgeGate: 0\n' > .yarnrc.yml \
 && CI=1 yarn add @schedjs/daemon@0.10.2 \
 && yarn cache clean
ENV PATH="/app/node_modules/.bin:${PATH}"
ENTRYPOINT ["schedd"]

We publish sched-daemon:<version> to our registry (ghcr.io/schedjs). Internal builds pull @schedjs/daemon from a private npm registry: the token is passed as a BuildKit secret (never an ARG/ENV — that would land in the image layers and docker history) and the registry is pointed at it for the duration of the install only:

# private-registry build (public builds omit the secret + registry arg)
docker build \
  --secret id=registry_token,env=NPM_REGISTRY_TOKEN \
  --build-arg NPM_REGISTRY=https://registry.npmjs.org \
  -t ghcr.io/schedjs/sched-daemon:0.11.0 apps/daemon

npmMinimalAgeGate: 0 — yarn 4.18 quarantines packages whose publish-time metadata the private registry doesn't serve; the gate is a supply-chain nicety we can't satisfy against a private registry.

Storage adapters are composition

A daemon with a non-sqlite storage is a derived image: FROM the base and yarn add the adapter — the same node_modules the daemon dynamic-imports at runtime (--storage <kind>, CLI). A private npm registry needs a token for yarn add — pass it as a BuildKit secret (never an ARG/ENV: that lands in the image layers and docker history):

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
FROM ghcr.io/schedjs/sched-daemon:0.11.0
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=registry_token \
    printf 'nodeLinker: node-modules\nnpmMinimalAgeGate: 0\nnpmRegistryServer: "https://registry.npmjs.org"\nnpmAlwaysAuth: true\nnpmAuthToken: "%s"\n' "$(cat /run/secrets/registry_token)" > .yarnrc.yml \
 && CI=1 yarn add @schedjs/storage-mongo@0.5.0 \
 && rm -f .yarnrc.yml

# build it — the token enters via the secret mount, not a build arg
docker build --secret id=registry_token,env=NPM_REGISTRY_TOKEN -t schedd-mongo .

npmMinimalAgeGate: 0 is required against a private registry (yarn 4.18 quarantines packages whose publish-time metadata the private registry doesn't serve), and pin the adapter version explicitly — an unpinned yarn add @schedjs/storage-mongo can silently resolve an older version (age-gate window), and an adapter without createStorage(env) breaks --storage mongo at runtime (books T2 finding 2026-08-22). Pin: yarn add @schedjs/storage-mongo@0.5.0.

# run it — connstring only in env, never in arguments
docker run --rm -e MONGO_URL=mongodb://user:pass@db.internal:27017/sched \
  schedd-mongo --tasks /app/tasks.json --storage mongo

Same pattern for @schedjs/storage-mysql (MYSQL_URL) and @schedjs/storage-postgres (PG_URL). A custom adapter is an npm package (or a path mounted into the image) exporting createStorage(env): Promise<Storage> (BYO contract):

FROM ghcr.io/schedjs/sched-daemon:0.11.0
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=registry_token \
    printf '…registry block (see above)…' > .yarnrc.yml \
 && CI=1 yarn add my-org/sched-storage-redis \
 && rm -f .yarnrc.yml

docker run --rm schedd-mongo --tasks /app/tasks.json --storage my-org/sched-storage-redis

If the adapter package is missing from the image, the daemon fails fast with the exact fix (RUN yarn add @schedjs/storage-mongo).

Windows (git-bash) operators: docker run with POSIX-style container paths mangles /app/… and /data/… into C:/Program Files/Git/… (→ unable to open database file). Prefix the command with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 (or use PowerShell / cmd).

Docker stack (dev)

docker-compose.dev.yml at the repo root runs two services:

ServiceImagePortsNotes
daemonbuilt from apps/daemon/Dockerfile (npm-based, --storage ready)8080--admin-host 0.0.0.0, SCHED_ADMIN_KEY=dev-key, healthcheck with Bearer, SQLite in a volume
shellbuilt from packages/ui/Dockerfile.serve8095 → 8081sched-ui serve: static UI + proxies /api → daemon
docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml up --build

Web UI: http://127.0.0.1:8095 (shell) · Admin API: http://127.0.0.1:8080 (daemon).

Security model

Auth lives at the boundaries — a private network is not authorization:

  • Admin API / UI — SCHED_ADMIN_KEY (Bearer). In production the daemon binds 127.0.0.1/private network, and a reverse proxy (traefik) terminates TLS.
  • Docker runner — image allowlist (exact + prefix*, fail-fast before spawn) and a read-only docker-socket proxy (POST=0) instead of a raw socket.
  • HTTP runner — outbound x-sched-api-key per task (see HTTP runner).

Production deployment (VDS)

Recommended layout behind traefik:

traefik ── basicAuth / forwardAuth ──▶ shell (static UI) + /api
                                         │
daemon ── listens 127.0.0.1 / private ──┘  (SCHED_ADMIN_KEY = second layer)
docker runner ──▶ docker-socket proxy (tecnativa, POST=0) + image allowlist
  • Terminate TLS at traefik; protect the shell + /api with basicAuth (or forwardAuth), SCHED_ADMIN_KEY adds a second layer.
  • The daemon never listens on a public interface.
  • Deployment artifacts go through the standard admin flow (Portainer, traefik labels).

Pausing the queue

A running daemon can be frozen with one action and released later — no restart, no dead tasks.json sync, no dead retention. The freeze is runtime state, not data: it is deliberately not persisted, so a restart always comes back in the state the operator asked for at boot.

Start frozen — boot ordering (DB migrations, worker deploy) where a startup catch-up burst would hit a half-ready world:

docker run -e SCHED_START_PAUSED=1 ... schedd --tasks tasks.json

SCHED_START_PAUSED=1 sets the initial state only. Release the queue through the control plane (engine.resume() embedded; the admin API / CLI surface ships with the same wave). There is intentionally no --start-paused CLI flag: the env is the one flag, and compose / Portainer can pass it where a flag cannot be appended. With the env unset the daemon starts active, exactly as before.

While paused the engine claims nothing new. Everything that is not a claim keeps running: tasks.json sync, retention/prune, the async poll loop and alerts for runs already in flight — a pause is a queue brake, not docker stop.

One caveat: the freeze is per daemon process. The flag lives in the engine, not in storage, so with two daemons pointed at the same database POST /queue/pause freezes only the daemon that served the request while its sibling keeps claiming. Several daemons against one database is not a supported topology today (the SQL adapters assume a single writer and their migrations are not lock-guarded); if it becomes one, the pause flag has to move into storage.

Why pause = skip, not catch-up

On release, a recurring schedule (cron / interval) whose slot came due while paused is skipped: nextRunAt moves to the next future slot via the ordinary next-slot calculation, and no missed-slot fires for the paused window (the slot was dropped on purpose, not lost). Overdue one-shots (once, a deferred at) and pending retries are kept and played exactly once — they carry an operator intent, and silently dropping them loses work.

Catch-up was rejected on purpose. Pause overnight and catch-up means every schedule fires at once in the morning, each one reported as a missed-slot, against whatever concurrency the box has — the classic thundering herd, plus an alert storm caused by the operator. "Pause = turn the daemon off" was rejected too: tasks.json sync, retention and in-flight alerts would die with it, and a pause would be indistinguishable from docker stop. Skip semantics is the honest contract: missed slots are missed. To run one on demand, trigger the task by hand (sched trigger <task>).

Status alerts

sched can push a notification when a run reaches a terminal state — failed by (default) — or when a schedule slot fired late (missed-slot, see below). The channel is a single universal outbound webhook (HTTP POST + JSON): the de-facto standard every external world speaks — Slack / Discord / Teams / Telegram / ntfy / PagerDuty are all POSTs with different JSON, so one endpoint covers them all. This is the platform-level signal that something finished (and how); content emails and artifact generation stay with the runner (who generates what).

Configure it two ways — the daemon accepts an alerts option in its createDaemon options, or (binary workflow, no code) a top-level alerts block in tasks.json (schedd --tasks tasks.json picks it up like it picks up runners). A programmatic alerts option overrides the file block:

createDaemon({
  tasksPath: 'tasks.json',
  dbPath: 'sched.db',
  alerts: {
    on: ['failed'],   // default — alert on failures only (also: 'succeeded', 'cancelled')
    onMissed: true,   // default — alert on late schedule slots too; set false to silence
    onSyncFailed: true, // default — alert when the tasks.json sync fails (see below); set false to silence
    onStreak: 3,      // optional — alert once per 3-failure streak instead of every failure (default 1 = today's behaviour)
    webhook: {
      url: 'https://hooks.example.com/sched',
      secret: 'whsec_…',              // optional — enables HMAC signature (see below)
      headers: { 'X-Ops-Token': '…' }, // optional — extra headers for your service
      timeoutMs: 10_000,               // optional — per-attempt timeout, default 10s
    },
    tasks: {                          // optional — per-task routing overrides
      'generate-thumbnail': { on: [] },      // silence a cosmetic task
      'sync-payments': { webhook: { url: 'https://hooks.example.com/pagerduty' } }, // different channel
    },
  },
  missedSlotGraceMs: 120_000, // optional — how late a dispatch must be to count as missed (default 2 min)
});

Sync health — sync.failed. The daemon re-reads tasks.json on the sync interval and reconciles. When that sync fails (storage unreachable — a dead mongo pool means nothing schedules, so a run.failed alert could never fire; or a broken file), the daemon POSTs sync.failed to the webhook. Payload:

{ "version": 1, "event": "sync.failed", "error": "…", "consecutiveFailures": 1 }

Only the first failure of a streak fires (dedupe) — a storage that stays down for a day does not spam one alert per 60s sync tick. When a sync succeeds, the streak resets and the next incident alerts again.

Streak — one alert per incident. onStreak (default 1) is the number of consecutive persistent failures that makes a task an incident worth a message (a failure with a retry still scheduled is not counted on its own — the whole retry ladder is one incident; its depth shows up as run.attempt):

  • onStreak: 1 → no gate: every terminal failure alerts — the behaviour every deployment had before this option existed, so an upgrade that changes nothing in config changes nothing in the inbox.
  • onStreak: N > 1 → the failure alert fires exactly once per streak, when the N-th consecutive failure lands. Failures 2..N stay silent, and so does the rest of the streak (no reminders — consecutiveFailures is in the payload, and the FAILS column in sched tasks shows how many failures the task has accumulated: the task row plus its schedule rows, since a schedule-fired run advances the schedule, not the task. It is not the streak itself — the streak lives in the engine process, below). A success breaks the streak: the next incident alerts again.
  • «Отпустило» (recovery) — the success that broke a streak which had reached the threshold carries previousFailures (how many failures it ended). It is a run.succeeded alert like any other, so it is gated by on: with the default on: ['failed'] no success notification is sent — add 'succeeded' to receive the release signal. A success below the threshold stays a plain run.succeeded, and a cancelled run neither counts nor breaks a streak.

The streak is counted in the daemon process (the storage failCount is cumulative — it never resets on success — and a persisted consecutive-counter would be a Storage-contract change): a restart forgets an in-flight streak, so the count restarts from 1 and with onStreak: N > 1 an incident already in progress does not alert on the next failure — it re-alerts only after another N−1 terminal failures, with consecutiveFailures: N (the post-restart count, not the true depth). The cost is lateness, never silence: no alert is lost for good. Per-task override: one alerts block per task, same field (onStreak merges field-wise, task wins). onSyncFailed is root-only — sync health is daemon-global, not a per-task property.

Per-task routing. The root alerts block is the channel + defaults; a task can override its own routing with a task-level alerts block in tasks.json (or the tasks map above for the programmatic path) — field-wise merge, task wins, arrays replace:

{
  "tasks": [
    { "name": "generate-thumbnail", "runner": "internal", "alerts": { "on": [] } },
    { "name": "sync-payments", "runner": "http", "alerts": { "webhook": { "url": "https://hooks.example.com/pagerduty" } } }
  ],
  "alerts": {
    "on": ["failed"],
    "onMissed": true,
    "webhook": { "url": "https://hooks.example.com/sched", "secret": "whsec_…" }
  }
}
  • generate-thumbnail (on: []) stays silent on failure — the root on does not apply to it. A task without an alerts block keeps the root defaults.
  • sync-payments keeps the root on/onMissed but routes to its own webhook — the multi-channel escape hatch for criticality ≠ channel.
  • Malformed task alerts fails at load (see Tasks → Per-task alert routing); the root alerts block is validated by the same rules (on/onMissed/onSyncFailed/onStreak/webhook, plus the per-task tasks map it may carry) — a typo like onStreak: 0 or onSyncFailed: "yes" stops the daemon at startup instead of silently disabling alerting.

Instead of SQLite you can hand the daemon any storage adapter (see Storage) — pass storage and omit dbPath:

const storage = await createMysqlStorage(pool); // or postgres / mongo / custom
createDaemon({ tasksPath: 'tasks.json', storage, alerts: { … } });

At the binary level the same choice is --storage (see CLI → Storage selection) — the daemon builds the storage from the connstring env, no code.

const storage = await createMysqlStorage(pool); // or postgres / mongo / custom
createDaemon({ tasksPath: 'tasks.json', storage, alerts: { … } });

Payload

Every POST carries a JSON body with a version (starts at 1 — bump-proof your consumer against evolution) and an event discriminator.

Terminal run states — event is run.<status> (run.failed / run.succeeded / run.cancelled):

{
  "version": 1,
  "event": "run.failed",
  "consecutiveFailures": 3,
  "task": { "name": "publish-video", "runner": "http" },
  "run": {
    "id": "9f1c…",
    "status": "failed",
    "attempt": 3,
    "error": "connection refused",
    "startedAt": "2026-08-19T09:00:00.000Z",
    "finishedAt": "2026-08-19T09:00:01.000Z"
  }
}

consecutiveFailures rides at the top level (next to event, like sync.failed) and is present on failure alerts only. The success that ends a streak which reached onStreak carries previousFailures instead:

{
  "version": 1,
  "event": "run.succeeded",
  "previousFailures": 3,
  "task": { "name": "publish-video", "runner": "http" },
  "run": { "id": "a41e…", "status": "succeeded", "attempt": 1, "error": null, "startedAt": "2026-08-20T09:00:00.000Z", "finishedAt": "2026-08-20T09:00:02.000Z" }
}

Missed slot — a schedule dispatched more than the grace window after its slot (downtime catch-up, wedged lock):

{
  "version": 1,
  "event": "missed-slot",
  "task": { "name": "publish-video", "runner": "http" },
  "schedule": { "id": "publish-video#0", "scheduledAt": "2026-08-19T09:00:00.000Z", "delayMs": 32400000 }
}

Signature (HMAC)

When webhook.secret is set, sched signs the exact request body with HMAC-SHA256 and sends it as X-Sched-Signature-256:

X-Sched-Signature-256: sha256=<hex>

Verify on your side (Node):

import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';

function verify(secret: string, body: string, sig: string | undefined): boolean {
  if (!sig?.startsWith('sha256=')) return false;
  const expected = createHmac('sha256', secret).update(body).digest();
  const received = Buffer.from(sig.slice('sha256='.length), 'hex');
  return received.length === expected.length && timingSafeEqual(received, expected);
}

No secret → the POST is unsigned (plain webhook, e.g. into a chat gateway).

Delivery semantics

  • Bounded retry, never fails the run flow. Up to 3 attempts total with backoff 5s / 30s. Network errors, timeouts and 5xx are retried; 4xx is not (a config error on the sender's side — retrying is pointless, it logs and stops). Exhausted → [alerts] error log. The run itself is never affected.
  • Persistent failure = the alert point. A failed run that still has retries scheduled does not alert — the notification lands only on the final, exhausted failure (Tasks → retry). Manual triggerTask alerts immediately and never auto-retries. With onStreak: N > 1 that point is the N-th consecutive failure (see above); the alert fires once, not once per run.
  • Missed-slot semantics. A schedule with run history dispatched more than missedSlotGraceMs (default 2 min) after its slot fires missed-slot — engine down at the slot / wedged lock / long queue. The signal is cause-agnostic: tune the grace up if your engine legitimately queues runs longer than that. Freshly created schedules never fire it — a new schedule's first slot is always in the future (past slots are never catch-up-dispatched), and the check additionally requires run history (lastRunAt), so a history-less schedule that is ever dispatched late (e.g. a one-shot with at in the past) is not reported as a miss either. If the daemon itself is down, detection happens on restart — an external uptime monitor covers the gap.
  • Embedded / any engine — same hooks: onRunFinal: createAlerts(config).handleFinal plus onEvent: createAlerts(config).handleEvent (see Logging → terminal events).

CLI/env wiring for alerts is not implemented yet — the surfaces are the createDaemon({ alerts }) option and the tasks.json alerts block. On request it becomes a daemon flag / SCHED_ALERTS_* env.

Storage

SQLite by default (single file, --db). MySQL/MariaDB, Postgres and Mongo are available as storage adapters (shared history across replicas) via --storage — see CLI → Storage selection and Storage.
